grade.primary_choice: Keep .NET isolated worker, move this app to Flex Consumption with always-ready instances, measure first, tune startup
unsupported_claims: States as fact that '.NET is slower to cold-start than Node or Go'. The reference says a tuned .NET isolated app and a Node app have broadly comparable cold starts on Consumption, because the platform's own startup dominates.
Calls Go via custom handler the 'fastest cold start' without noting that the Functions host still has to cold-start.

'Most teams find the time is in their own startup code... not in the runtime' is a generalisation with no support, and it skips the platform's share (instance allocation, mounting the package, starting the host).
grade.notes: Sound, well-hedged recommendation that matches the reference: stay on .NET isolated, fix cold starts through Flex always-ready instances or Premium, measure first, tune startup, check provider rate limits, and fall back to AKS with KEDA. It loses points for conceding that .NET is inherently slower instead of explaining that platform startup dominates, and for not saying the steady traffic already keeps one instance warm, pre-scaling ahead of sale days, or that only this app needs paid warm capacity.
